analysis.one_liner: Bans the EPA from spending any money to regulate carbon dioxide.
analysis.headline: The one-paragraph bill to cut off all EPA funding for carbon dioxide rules never left a House subcommittee and died when the 111th Congress ended, having attracted only a sponsor and two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter's bill was a single sentence: no matter what any other law says, the EPA could not spend a dime regulating carbon dioxide emissions. If it had passed, it would have shut down every EPA effort to limit the pollution most responsible for climate change, from power plants to vehicles, without offering any replacement policy. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal-burning power plants, oil refiners, coal producers, and other large emitters of carbon dioxide. The bill would have barred the EPA from spending any money on carbon dioxide regulation, sparing them compliance costs, potential shutdown or retrofit requirements, and the uncertainty of pending federal greenhouse gas rules, while leaving no alternative federal climate policy in place.

how_it_helps.text: It would have cut off all EPA spending on carbon dioxide regulation, freeing power plants, refineries, and other major emitters from any federal limits on their largest greenhouse gas and freeing them from compliance costs, retrofits, or operating restrictions.

It did so with a blanket prohibition that overrode any other provision of law, so no court ruling, existing rule, or future act of Congress could have restored EPA carbon rules while it was in effect.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people. Stripping the EPA of any ability to regulate carbon dioxide would have left the public without federal limits on the pollution driving climate change, with the health and disaster costs that follow, while the industries responsible avoided the bill. The bill contained no replacement policy, so the cost would simply have shifted from emitters to everyone else.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through pollution and climate costs

drawbacks.text: The bill's strongest good-faith argument was that regulating carbon dioxide under the Clean Air Act could raise energy prices and burden manufacturing jobs, and that climate policy should be written by Congress rather than by an agency. But the bill offered no alternative climate legislation, so its effect would have been to leave carbon emissions unregulated entirely.

Even a supporter would have to acknowledge the breadth of the prohibition: by barring every dollar for carbon dioxide regulation 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' it would have blocked the EPA from carrying out any carbon-related duty, however modest, rather than targeting any specific rule deemed overly costly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the industries the bill served, the benefit was direct and measurable: no federal carbon rules and no compliance costs. For the public, the cost was the loss of the government's only working tool for limiting carbon pollution, with no substitute. The bill was not a redesign of climate policy but a deletion of it, and the public cost outweighed the industry gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2009, referred to committee and then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, so it never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter introduced the bill on December 16, 2009, with Reps. Dan Burton and Pat Tiberi as the only cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, where it stayed; the record shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor action ever took place.
The bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, leaving the EPA's authority to regulate carbon dioxide untouched.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the EPA kept its authority and funding to regulate carbon dioxide, so the public's existing protections remained intact. The industries that would have been exempted from carbon rules — power plants, refiners, and coal producers — did not get the relief they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept EPA carbon rules

for.name: Rep. Thaddeus McCotter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar the EPA from spending any money on carbon dioxide regulation.

for.name: Reps. Dan Burton and Pat Tiberi

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Henry Waxman
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill went to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment and saw no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only three House Republicans put their names on the bill and no Democrat did, but since it never reached a hearing or a vote there is no roll call showing where each party actually stood.

industries.note: Power plants are the largest source of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions, and the bill would have barred the EPA from spending anything to regulate those emissions, eliminating compliance costs and any threat of operating limits. The industry's gain would have come directly at the expense of air quality and climate protection for the public.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refineries and fuel combustion are major carbon dioxide sources facing EPA greenhouse gas rules; the funding ban would have shielded them from federal limits with no replacement policy. Their savings would have been paid for in pollution borne by the public.

Most coal is burned in power plants, so blocking EPA carbon regulation would have protected demand for coal against rules that make it more expensive to burn. The benefit to the industry would have come at the cost of the public's exposure to emissions and mining-related pollution.
